evidence.claim: Along Alameda Creek, two railway lines share a narrow canyon.
evidence.quote: Two railroads also follow the same route down the canyon from Sunol to Niles

evidence.claim: Along Alameda Creek, two railway lines share a narrow canyon.
evidence.quote: Parts of the valley are extremely narrow and are referred to as Niles Canyon

evidence.claim: Niles Canyon Road follows Alameda Creek’s canyon between Fremont’s Niles district and Sunol.
evidence.quote: The stretch of State Route 84 known as Niles Canyon Road traverses the length of the canyon from the Niles district of Fremont to the unincorporated town of Sunol.

evidence.claim: Niles Canyon Road follows Alameda Creek’s canyon between Fremont’s Niles district and Sunol.
evidence.quote: Niles Canyon is a canyon in the San Francisco Bay Area formed by Alameda Creek

evidence.claim: Parts of the valley are extremely narrow.
evidence.quote: Parts of the valley are extremely narrow and are referred to as Niles Canyon

evidence.claim: Caltrans designates Route 84 from Route 238 to I-680 as a scenic highway, under criteria calling for a “memorable landscape” without “visual intrusions.”
evidence.quote: is designated as a scenic highway by the California Department of Transportation from SR 238 to I-680 in Alameda County, meaning that it is a substantial section of highway passing through a "memorable landscape" with no "visual intrusions"

evidence.claim: The road connects Sunol and Fremont in seven miles, alongside both a heritage railway and an active Union Pacific mainline.
evidence.quote: Niles Canyon Road runs westward from Sunol and is a scenic 7-mile (11 km) drive to Fremont.

evidence.claim: The road connects Sunol and Fremont in seven miles, alongside both a heritage railway and an active Union Pacific mainline.
evidence.quote: The Union Pacific Railroad (formerly Western Pacific Railroad) has an active mainline on the south side of the canyon

evidence.claim: Before the highway, the overland route El Camino Viejo a Los Ángeles passed through the canyon.
evidence.quote: The route of El Camino Viejo a Los Ángeles (Old Road to Los Angeles), the oldest north-south trail in the interior of Alta California, ran through Niles Canyon.

evidence.claim: In September 1869, the first through train from Sacramento reached Alameda Terminal through this passage.
evidence.quote: The first through train from Sacramento to Alameda Terminal (the first terminus of the Transcontinental Railroad ) ran through Alameda Cañon on September 6, 1869.

evidence.claim: The line lost its transcontinental traffic to a shorter Benicia route in 1879.
evidence.quote: lost its transcontinental traffic in 1879 to a shorter route through Benicia.

evidence.claim: By around 1900, Niles attracted picnic day-trippers, and the name Niles Canyon replaced the earlier Alameda Cañon.
evidence.quote: As Niles became known as a picnic day-tripper destination around 1900, the name Niles Canyon replaced Alameda Cañon.

evidence.claim: A later Western Pacific line, built through the canyon in 1905–1908, required two tunnels and a steel bridge.
evidence.quote: when the Western Pacific tracks were laid through the canyon in 1905 to 1908, they were left with a more difficult challenge. This forced Western Pacific engineers to bore two tunnels and construct a steel bridge to lay their tracks.

evidence.claim: Begin at Niles, where the Vallejo Flour Mill ruins mark the canyon’s western end, then follow the creek toward Sunol.
evidence.quote: At the west end of the canyon are the ruins of the Vallejo Flour Mill

evidence.claim: The former Southern Pacific alignment follows the north side, now used by the Niles Canyon Railway; the newer Union Pacific line lies to the south.
evidence.quote: the old Southern Pacific track along the north side, now the Niles Canyon Railway, and the newer Union Pacific (formerly the Western Pacific) track a little to the south.

evidence.claim: Sunol lies near Alameda Creek at the northwest edge of the Sunol Valley.
evidence.quote: The town lies near Alameda Creek at the northwest edge of the Sunol Valley.

evidence.claim: Essanay’s Niles studio began in an empty barn in 1912. The following year the company built ten cottages for actors and a studio near the railroad tracks.
evidence.quote: In 1912 Anderson settled on a location in Niles Canyon in the San Francisco East Bay Area, setting up in Frank Mortimer's empty barn

evidence.claim: Essanay’s Niles studio began in an empty barn in 1912. The following year the company built ten cottages for actors and a studio near the railroad tracks.
evidence.quote: The next year in the town of Niles at the mouth of Niles Canyon, "Essanay built 10 modest cottages for their actors on 2nd Street, between F and G streets, and constructed an unassuming (200-foot) studio nearby", across the street from the railroad tracks.

evidence.claim: More than 350 Essanay films were made here, and Charlie Chaplin filmed The Tramp in the canyon.
evidence.quote: More than 350 films were produced in Niles by Essanay.

evidence.claim: More than 350 Essanay films were made here, and Charlie Chaplin filmed The Tramp in the canyon.
evidence.quote: it was here that Charlie Chaplin filmed one of his most iconic movies, The Tramp.

evidence.claim: Chaplin later moved his production unit to Los Angeles, disliking Niles’s chilly climate and Chicago’s unpredictable weather.
evidence.quote: Chaplin didn't like the unpredictable weather of Chicago or the chilly climate of Niles, and moved his production unit to the more temperate Los Angeles.

evidence.claim: The lot closed in 1916 and was demolished by the 1930s.
evidence.quote: On 16 February 1916, the Niles lot was closed by George K. Spoor via telegram. By the 1930s, it had been torn down.

evidence.claim: The Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum occupies the Edison Theater, half a block from the former studio site, preserving silent films and motion-picture equipment.
evidence.quote: The museum is housed in the Edison Theater building, a century-old Nickelodeon movie theater, just half a block from the former site of the Niles Essanay Studios

evidence.claim: The Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum occupies the Edison Theater, half a block from the former studio site, preserving silent films and motion-picture equipment.
evidence.quote: The museum houses a large collection of Motion Picture equipment and related artifacts, as well as about 10,000 Silent Films in their archive.

evidence.claim: A stone foundation survives from the second Vallejo Flour Mill, built in 1856 at the mouth of the canyon.
evidence.quote: A second Flour Mill was built in 1856, the stone foundation of which may still be seen today.

evidence.claim: José de Jesús Vallejo built the first mill in 1841, with a dam and aqueduct to provide power.
evidence.quote: The first Vallejo Flour Mill, in the Niles district of Fremont, California, was built in 1841 by José de Jesús Vallejo

evidence.claim: José de Jesús Vallejo built the first mill in 1841, with a dam and aqueduct to provide power.
evidence.quote: along with a dam and aqueduct to power it.

evidence.claim: A watercolor from 1856 by Vallejo’s daughter Carmelita depicts the three-story mill and its large wooden wheel.
evidence.quote: A watercolor painting of the 1856 Flour Mill, done by Carmelita Vallejo, J & J Vallejo's daughter then finishing her studies at the San Jose Notre Dame Academy, showed several buildings surrounding a three-story Flour Mill building with a large wooden wheel on the north side.

evidence.claim: Rail construction later displaced the waterworks: Vallejo’s aqueduct was torn out for the new line and rebuilt.
evidence.quote: followed the line of Vallejo's aqueduct, which was torn out to build the railroad and then rebuilt.

evidence.claim: In 1909, Southern Pacific demolished the original adobe mill to make room for a railway junction.
evidence.quote: In 1909, the 1841 adobe mill was torn down to make way for a wye-switch built by Southern Pacific Railroad.

evidence.claim: The ruins occupy Vallejo Mill Historical Park at Niles Canyon Road and Mission Boulevard.
evidence.quote: The ruins of the Vallejo Flour Mill is located at the northeast corner of Niles Canyon Road (State Route 84) and Mission Boulevard (State Route 238) in Vallejo Mill Historical Park.

evidence.claim: The surviving stone foundation belongs to the second mill, built in 1856.
evidence.quote: A second Flour Mill was built in 1856, the stone foundation of which may still be seen today.

evidence.claim: Chinese laborers built the railway bed into the canyon’s tight curves and narrow banks during the 1860s.
evidence.quote: The Western Pacific used 500 Chinese laborers to grade and construct the rail line into the rugged canyon with its tight curves and narrow banks.

evidence.claim: Their work included masonry culverts, retaining walls and bridge piers as well as wooden bridges.
evidence.quote: In addition to building wooden bridges and grading the railroad bed, the laborers built culverts, retaining walls, and bridge piers in masonry.

evidence.claim: Much of that stonework remains visible.
evidence.quote: Many of these stonework built by Chinese laborers in the late 1860s can still be seen today.

evidence.claim: Steel bridges replaced covered wooden spans at Farwell and Dresser, while original cut-stone abutments, culverts and retaining walls survived later rebuilding.
evidence.quote: Steel bridges replaced the covered timber bridges at Farwell and Dresser

evidence.claim: Steel bridges replaced covered wooden spans at Farwell and Dresser, while original cut-stone abutments, culverts and retaining walls survived later rebuilding.
evidence.quote: Despite these improvements, the few rebuilding programs by the railroad left the Niles Canyon line with many of its original cut-stone bridge abutments, culverts, and retaining walls

evidence.claim: After Southern Pacific ended operations in 1984, the Pacific Locomotive Association began rebuilding track in 1987.
evidence.quote: Southern Pacific ceased its operations through the canyon in 1984

evidence.claim: After Southern Pacific ended operations in 1984, the Pacific Locomotive Association began rebuilding track in 1987.
evidence.quote: The Pacific Locomotive Association leased the right of way from the county and began working to reconstruct the track in 1987.

evidence.claim: Its first passenger train left Sunol in May 1988. The heritage railway now uses both steam and diesel locomotives for public excursions.
evidence.quote: The Niles Canyon Railway ran its first passenger train from Sunol on May 21, 1988.

evidence.claim: Its first passenger train left Sunol in May 1988. The heritage railway now uses both steam and diesel locomotives for public excursions.
evidence.quote: The NCRy features public excursions with both steam and diesel locomotives

evidence.claim: Sunol’s 1884 depot combined passenger, freight and railway-agent facilities under one roof.
evidence.quote: Sunol Depot This one-story Stick style depot was built to Southern Pacific standard design No. 7 in 1884.

evidence.claim: Sunol’s 1884 depot combined passenger, freight and railway-agent facilities under one roof.
evidence.quote: A “combination depot” such as this housed facilities for a company agent, freight and passengers in one building

evidence.claim: It is the last survivor of at least eleven Southern Pacific No. 7 depots.
evidence.quote: Out of at least eleven No. 7 depots built by the railroad, Sunol is the last one remaining.

evidence.claim: The agent’s office has a five-window bay on the track side and a small ticket window opening into the passenger waiting room.
evidence.quote: The agents office is next to the west and features a five-window bay on the track side

evidence.claim: The agent’s office has a five-window bay on the track side and a small ticket window opening into the passenger waiting room.
evidence.quote: a small ticket window connects this office with the passenger waiting room.

evidence.claim: The freight-room floor was raised to match freight cars and teamsters’ wagons. That room now holds exhibits and meetings, while the building retains the arrangement that once brought several kinds of railroad business together.
evidence.quote: Finally, the freight room takes up the rest of the building and is set about forty inches above grade so that its floor would be level with the floor of freight cars and teamsters’ wagons. This room is now used for exhibits and meetings.

evidence.claim: A gable roof covers the east end; an elevated hip roof marks the freight room at the west.
evidence.quote: The roof is divided into two parts with a gable roof over the east end, and an elevated hip roof over the freight room to the west.
